title: Growth and Patterns of Tourism in India
summary: An international tourist is a person visiting India on a foreign passport who stays at least 24 hours for leisure, health, study, religion, sport, business or meeting friends without taking a paid job (diplomats and armed forces do not count). A domestic tourist travels within the country to a place other than the usual residence or work and stays at least 24 hours in accommodation; people visiting their home town for social functions do not count. Tourists spend nearly 40% of their money on handicrafts such as jewellery, carpets, leather, ivory and brass work. 'Atithi Devo Bhava' (guest is God) and Nehru's 'Welcome as a tourist and send them back as a friend' show India's tradition. India's tourism is natural (mountain, island, desert, coastal, lacustrine, wildlife, adventure) and cultural (religious, historical, traditional, health, sports, rural).

Health tourism (low-cost world-class treatment; ayurveda, naturopathy, unani, siddha; tourists from the US, Europe and the Middle East), spiritual tourism (India as the confluence of religions), adventure tourism (mostly at high altitude), MICE tourism (Meetings, Incentives, Conferences and Exhibitions, fast-growing since liberalisation in 1991), rural tourism (interaction with local people and their cultural life) and sustainable tourism (meeting present needs without harming future generations; minimum impact on the environment).

Growth can be positive (more tourists) or negative (fewer). Tourism grew rapidly after the second half of the 20th century and substantially after the 1990s because of the wealth and leisure time of tourists from rich countries and better transport, communication and accommodation. South Asia's high growth in 1990: India captures more than half of South Asia's tourist arrivals and about 75% of its receipts. Two main measures of the tourism index are international tourist arrivals and tourism receipts.

Factors affecting growth: geographical (climate, landscape, location: plains tourists go to hill stations in summer), cultural events (Durga Puja, Holi, Diwali, Goa Carnival, Dandiya, Desert Festival, Surajkund Mela, Onam), safety and security (Kashmir fell after 1985 because of terrorism), economic conditions (higher incomes travel more), facilities and services (accommodation, transport, banking, guides) and government policies (subsidies, packages and a liberal visa policy).

FTAs were only 16,829 in 1951 and rose to 1.14 million in 1981 and 6.30 million in 2011; they were 23.33 million in 2015 (the 4.4% growth); 2009 had a small fall and 2001–02 and 2012 also fell. India's share in international arrivals was 0.40% in 1997 and 0.64% in 2011 (below 1%). India's world rank improved from 54th in 2002 to 38th in 2011 and 24th in 2015 (the lesson also notes 52nd in the Travel and Tourism Competitiveness Report 2015). Top ten source countries in 2014: USA 14.57%, Bangladesh 12.27%, UK 10.92%, then Sri Lanka, Russia, Canada, Malaysia, France, Australia and Germany (61.54% together). Foreign tourists stay a little over a month. State share of foreign tourist visits in 2014: Tamil Nadu 20.6% (first), Maharashtra 19.4%, Uttar Pradesh, Delhi, Rajasthan, West Bengal, Kerala, Bihar, Karnataka and Haryana (2.4%, the lowest of the top ten). In 2011 Maharashtra led with 24.7%. The most popular monuments are the Taj Mahal, Qutub Minar and Agra Fort.

Growth of domestic tourism comes from rising income, purchasing power and the dynamic middle class. Domestic tourists were 159.88 million in 1997, 526.70 million in 2007 and 1,431.97 million in 2015. Top states in 2015: Tamil Nadu (23.3%), Uttar Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana, Madhya Pradesh, West Bengal, Gujarat and Rajasthan; the top five states account for about two-thirds (63.3%) of domestic visits; the top ten for about 84–85%.

Tourism is a 'smokeless industry' with a unique ability to earn foreign exchange (which helps the balance of trade). Money spent by tourists is tourist receipt. FEEs were US$ 16.56 billion in 2011 against 14.19 billion in 2010 (16.7% growth). India's share in world tourism receipts was 0.64% in 1997 and reached 1.61% in 2011. FEEs in January–April 2013 were US$ 6.878 billion against US$ 6.145 billion a year earlier (9.61% growth). Government steps: a tourist branch in 1949, a separate Tourism Department in 1957, the Tourism Development Council in 1958, planning from the Second Five Year Plan, the National Policy on Tourism in 1982, industry status in the Seventh Plan (1985–90), the Mohammad Yunus Committee in 1988 (the foundation stone of Indian tourism), the National Action Plan in 1992, the National Strategy in 1996 and a separate Ministry of Tourism from 14 May 2000; the Incredible India campaign.

objective: Fill in the blanks. (a) The tourism index is measured by international tourist arrivals and ________. (b) Among all the monuments, the Taj Mahal, the Agra Fort and ________ are the most popular tourist sites.

Identify True or False. (a) Tourist arrivals means the number of persons who get accommodation at a tourist centre for at least 48 hours. (b) Foreign tourist arrivals in India are measured with tourism receipts as the other main index.
(a) False: the stay is at least 24 hours. (b) True: the two main measures are arrivals and receipts.

Fill in the blanks. (a) Tourism is a smokeless industry with a unique quality of earning ________ exchange. (b) On 14 May ________ the Government of India declared the Ministry of Tourism a separate ministry.

Identify True or False. (a) About two-thirds of domestic tourists are contributed by five states: Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh, Karnataka, Maharashtra and Andhra Pradesh. (b) The number of foreign tourists arriving in India is continuously increasing.
(a) True. (b) True (with small falls in some years).

Fill in the blanks. (a) The foreign exchange earnings during January–April 2013 were US$ 6.878 billion and in the same period of 2012 US$ ________ billion. (b) India captures more than half of the tourist arrivals and about ________ of the tourist receipts of South Asia.
Identify True or False. (a) Foreign tourist arrivals in India are continuously decreasing. (b) Tourism is a smokeless industry with a unique quality of earning foreign exchange.
Fill in the blanks. (a) The ranking of India in world tourism improved from 38th position (2011) to ________ in 2015. (b) India is a major tourist destination among the ________ nations.
Identify True or False. (a) India is a major tourist destination among the South Asian nations. (b) Tourism in India has not grown substantially since the beginning of the 1990s.
(a) True. (b) False: it has grown substantially.
Identify True or False. (a) Diplomats posted in a foreign country are called tourists. (b) India is a country known for its friendly treatment to all visitors.

Identify True or False. (a) In 2014 the country from which India received the largest number of foreign tourists was the UK. (b) The share of foreign tourists in India is less than 1% of world tourists.
(a) False: it was the USA. (b) True.

vsa: Why did travel and tourism increase in recent decades in India? Explain any two reasons.
Rich countries' tourists had better finances and more leisure time for holidays and business trips. Better transport, accessibility, communication and accommodation also encouraged travel.

or: Explain spiritual tourism as an emerging dimension in India in two points.
India is the confluence of Hinduism, Sikhism, Islam, Christianity, Buddhism and Jainism. Temples, mosques, monasteries and churches attract a huge number of domestic and international tourists.

vsa: 'The trend of international tourist arrivals is almost continuously on the rise.' Support the statement with two arguments.
Arrivals rose from 16,829 in 1951 to 6.3 million in 2011 and 23.33 million in 2015. Only a few years such as 2001, 2002, 2009 and 2012 saw small falls.

Describe any two features of a domestic tourist.

A domestic tourist travels within the country to a place other than the usual residence or work. The person stays in accommodation for at least 24 hours for leisure, pilgrimage, sports, health or study.
April 2026
Mention any two measures to boost tourism.
Government can give subsidies, packages and a liberal visa policy. Better infrastructure, safety and security and promotional shows abroad attract tourists.
April 2025
Differentiate between a domestic and an international tourist.

A domestic tourist travels within his own country and stays at least 24 hours away from home. An international tourist visits another country on a foreign passport and stays at least 24 hours without a paid job.
Write a short note on MICE tourism.
MICE means Meetings, Incentives, Conferences and Exhibitions. It has grown fast since the economic liberalisation of 1991 and India has the infrastructure for business tourists.
Explain the term 'health tourism'.
It is tourism for medical treatment, offering world-class treatment at low cost in ayurveda, naturopathy, unani, siddha and allopathy. It attracts patients from the US, Europe and the Middle East.
What is meant by growth of tourism? State its two types.
Growth of tourism is the change in the number of tourists. Positive growth means more tourists than before and negative growth means fewer.
Give two reasons for the growth of domestic tourism in India.
Rising income levels and purchasing power have grown. The emergence of a dynamic middle class has pushed domestic travel.
Which are the top three states in domestic tourists in 2015? Name them.
Tamil Nadu (23.3%), Uttar Pradesh (14.3%) and Andhra Pradesh (8.4%).
sa: 'The spatial distribution of tourism is a function of various environmental conditions.' Support the statement with three arguments.

(i) Climate sends plains tourists to hill stations in summer and cold-area tourists to warm places in winter. (ii) Landscape and geographical diversity (mountains, coasts, deserts) attract tourists to particular regions. (iii) Location and natural attractions decide the share of states: the top ten states get about 85% of domestic tourists.
Explain any three features of health tourism.

(i) It offers world-class treatment at low cost. (ii) It includes the Indian systems of medicine such as ayurveda, naturopathy, unani and siddha along with allopathy. (iii) It attracts patients from the US, Europe and the Middle East where treatment is costly.
Explain the concept of sustainable tourism in three points.

(i) It meets the needs of the present without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs. (ii) It keeps the impact of tourist activity on the environment to a minimum. (iii) It balances economic, social and environmental needs.
Describe the pattern of foreign tourist arrivals in India (three points).

(i) In 2014 the USA (14.57%), Bangladesh (12.27%) and the UK (10.92%) were the top source countries. (ii) The top ten countries gave about 61.5% of the arrivals. (iii) Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh and Delhi received most foreign tourists and tourists stay a little over a month.
Explain any three government initiatives for the promotion of tourism.

(i) A separate Tourism Department (1957), the Tourism Development Council (1958) and a Ministry of Tourism (2000). (ii) National Policy 1982, industry status in 1985–90, the Yunus Committee in 1988 and the National Action Plan in 1992. (iii) Incredible India campaign and simplified approvals for tour operators.
la: Explain any six factors affecting the growth of tourism.

(i) Geographical: climate, landscape and location decide the seasons and flows. (ii) Cultural events such as Durga Puja, Onam and Surajkund Mela attract crowds. (iii) Safety and security: tragedies reduce arrivals, as in Kashmir after 1985. (iv) Economic conditions: high-income people travel more. (v) Facilities and services: accommodation, transport, banking and guides. (vi) Government policies: subsidies, packages and a liberal visa policy.
Explain six points of the emerging dimensions of Indian tourism.

(i) Health tourism offers low-cost world-class treatment. (ii) Spiritual tourism draws pilgrims to temples, mosques, churches and monasteries. (iii) Adventure tourism grows in high-altitude areas. (iv) MICE tourism has grown since 1991 with improved facilities. (v) Rural tourism lets tourists interact with local people and culture. (vi) Sustainable tourism minimises the impact on the environment.
Discuss the growth and patterns of foreign and domestic tourists in India, in six points.

(i) FTAs rose from 16,829 in 1951 to 23.33 million in 2015. (ii) India's rank improved from 54th (2002) to 38th (2011) and 24th (2015), but its share stays below 1%. (iii) The USA, Bangladesh and the UK send the most; Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra receive the most foreign visitors. (iv) Domestic tourists grew from 159.88 million (1997) to 1,431.97 million (2015). (v) Tamil Nadu (23.3%) and Uttar Pradesh lead; five states give about 63% of domestic visits. (vi) FEEs were US$ 16.56 billion in 2011 and the government supports growth through the Ministry of Tourism.
